title: Methodology to calculate forest stand level maximum potential productivity, potential achievable productivity and ecosystem fit
author: Klock, Vogt, et al.

steps.title: Collect field and remote‑sensing data
steps.instruction: Gather (1) direct field measures of total net primary productivity (tNppobs) and site‑level environmental conditions (climatic, edaphic, biotic), (2) high‑resolution average monthly/daily temperature and solar radiation rasters for each site’s geographic coordinates (use buffer zones if point data are unavailable), and (3) the average annual atmospheric CO₂ concentration for the year of data collection (1981‑2011) from the Mauna Loa Observatory (https://www.sealevel.info/co2.html).

steps.title: Load raster data and extract site values
steps.instruction: In R, load the required packages, read the CSV of site coordinates, create raster stacks for temperature and solar radiation files, rename layers to month names, extract raster values at each site, convert to data frames, and set all negative values to NA.

steps.title: Determine growing season metrics
steps.instruction: Combine temperature and solar data, identify months with mean temperature > 0 °C (growing season), compute the number of grow days per month, and calculate seasonal averages of temperature and solar radiation.

substeps.instruction: tempsol$GrowTemp <- rowMeans(tempsol[ , month], na.rm = TRUE)   # mean temperature of growing season
tempsol$GrowSolar <- rowMeans(tempsol[ , month.srad], na.rm = TRUE)   # mean solar radiation of growing season
tempsol$GrowDays <- rowSums(tempsol[ , grep("GrowDays", names(tempsol))])   # total growing days

steps.title: Define physiological constants
steps.instruction: Set the model parameters used in all subsequent calculations.

substeps.instruction: R <- 0.008314   # kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (molar gas constant)
K <- 18.2       # MJ kg⁻¹, inverse specific energy of plant biomass
Ca <- 400       # ppm, standard atmospheric CO₂ concentration
Ci <- Ca * 0.7  # = 280 ppm, intercellular CO₂ concentration
beta <- 0.45    # fraction of absorbed quanta reaching PSII
alpha <- 0.9    # interception efficiency εi (canopy absorbs 90% of PAR)
Ei <- 0.9       # same as α for use in tNpptmax equation
PAR_frac <- 0.45   # PAR is 45% of total solar radiation

steps.title: Calculate photosynthetic parameters
steps.instruction: Using the growing‑season temperature (Gt) and the constants above, compute the photorespiration compensation point (γ), the rubisco‑limited carboxylation rate (Wi), net CO₂ uptake (A), and the conversion efficiency (Ec).

steps.title: Derive theoretical maximum NPP (tNpptmax)
steps.instruction: Combine seasonal solar radiation, growing‑season length, and physiological efficiencies to obtain the site‑specific theoretical maximum net primary productivity.

substeps.instruction: tempsol$tNpptmax <- tempsol$GrowSolar * tempsol$GrowDays * PAR_frac * Ei * tempsol$Ec * K   # units conversion to Mg ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ applied as needed

steps.title: Calculate Ecosystem Fit (eFit)
steps.instruction: Compute the percentage of observed productivity relative to the theoretical maximum.

steps.title: Optional: Random Forest analysis and validation
steps.instruction: If desired, model the relationship between eFit and environmental variables using Random Forest and validate the results.

description:
The “Ecosystem Fit” (eFit) of a forest [8] is the ratio of tNppobs/tNpptmax (where tNppobs = total net primary productivity measured at each site and tNpptmax = theoretical maximum potential total net primary productivity possible when there are no limits to growth), each in units of dry biomass (Mg ha−1 yr−1) in this paper. It expresses how well a forest is adapted to its site and its potential for growth, i.e., is it possible to grow more biomass than what is measured in the field. Ecosystem Fit [7] directly compares the measured tNpp (or tNppobs as used in this paper) to growth that is theoretically possible for that site without site-level constraints (i.e., tNpptmax as used in this paper). Current measures of tNpp do not allow an assessment of how vulnerable a forest is to climate change since this metric does not identify ranked thresholds of low, medium, or high tNpp by site (sensu
[9], [21]). In addition, tNpp does not inform how well forests perform in relation to site limiting factors. Thus, comparison of sites requires a productivity metric that defines the maximum potential productivity for each site. For example, forest stand-level comparisons for management strategies could be misleading as an internal reference of gross carbon flux since it could differ unpredictably between sites due to the variability of stand-specific factors affecting productive capacity. Whereas calculating eFit of an ecosystem relative to its current environment can be obtained with the calculation of tNpptmax as a reference condition to assess the potential of any site to grow biomass [7,8]. Since photosynthesis is the ecophysiological framework where carbon assimilation occurs, it is an indicator to quantify the environment's functional limitations on production [8,14]. Trees convert solar energy into biomass within their genetic and environmental constraints.
